posts.title: The sweets of November
posts.excerpt: A maple leaf that has just turned and a camellia that has not yet opened: two sweets for the month the hearth comes back.
posts.content:
In November the sunken hearth is opened again after the summer, and tea people call it the new year of tea. The sweets follow: the last maple leaves, and the first camellia buds.

Our sweet maker pushes white bean paste through a fine sieve for the camellia and tints the maple with a little persimmon. Eat it in three bites, with the pick, before the tea arrives.

posts.title: Why the kettle sings
posts.excerpt: Small iron pieces in the bottom of the kettle make the water hum like wind in pines. Getting the charcoal right is how you choose the moment.
posts.content:
Tea people call the sound matsukaze, wind in the pines. It comes from a few pieces of iron fixed under the kettle’s floor. When the water nears the boil, they hum.

In the charcoal class we lay three sizes of charcoal so the hum begins just as the guests sit down, and fades while the thick tea is kneaded. It takes about a year to get the timing right.

posts.title: One camellia for the alcove
posts.excerpt: Tea flowers are picked, not arranged: one bud, one leaf, a slim bamboo vase, and the rest left to the room.
posts.content:
Kazue picks the flower on her way to the tea room, from the hedge by the stone steps. A camellia goes in half open, so that it opens a little more while the guests are inside.

Students sometimes ask why there is only one. Look at it for the length of a bowl of tea and the question goes away.
